## Copper smelting and bronze `copper_bronze`
- Deps: needs charcoal_burning; helped by bellows_piston_blower, lost_wax_casting, refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: Green and blue copper ores (malachite, azurite) heated with charcoal in a small clay furnace under a forced blast give up metallic copper, which melts at 1085 °C; sulphide ores must first be roasted in the open to burn off the sulphur. Copper alone is soft and casts badly. About one part tin to nine of copper gives bronze, which melts lower, fills moulds and is much harder; more tin (20 % and above) gives brittle bell and mirror metal. Hammering hardens copper and bronze, and heating to redness softens them again, whether they are quenched or not.
- Pitfalls: Expecting quenching to harden bronze as it does steel; it does the opposite or nothing. | Damp moulds or damp charge: molten metal on water explodes. | Tin ore is rare (Cornwall, the Erzgebirge, Afghanistan, Malaya, Bolivia); most regions must trade for it. | Arsenical copper ores give a good early bronze but the fumes cripple the smiths. | Thinking a campfire is enough; without a blast and an enclosed furnace the ore will not reduce.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 8000 BC – hammered native copper in Anatolia (Çayönü); c. 5000 BC smelting in Anatolia and Iran; c. 3000 BC tin bronze in Mesopotamia; europe: c. 5000 BC – smelting at Belovode (Serbia), among the oldest known; c. 2200 BC tin bronze widespread; egypt: c. 4000 BC copper tools; arsenical copper through the Old Kingdom; tin bronze common from c. 2000 BC; india: c. 2600 BC – Harappan copper and bronze, including lost-wax figures; china: c. 2800 BC – earliest bronze knife (Majiayao); c. 1700 BC Erlitou and then Shang piece-mould casting of ritual vessels; americas: c. 4000 BC or earlier – hammered native copper around the Great Lakes; Andean smelting in the 1st millennium BC, arsenical bronze by c. AD 300, tin bronze c. AD 700; africa: c. 800–400 BC – copper smelting at Akjoujt (Mauritania) and in Niger (older Niger dates disputed); 9th c. AD lost-wax bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu
- Read: R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976) | Miljana Radivojević et al., On the origins of extractive metallurgy: new evidence from Europe, Journal of Archaeological Science 37 (2010)

## Bloomery iron (wrought iron, forging, carburising) `bloomery_iron`
- Deps: needs charcoal_burning; helped by bellows_piston_blower, copper_bronze, refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: Iron ore (bog ore, red or brown ironstone), roasted and broken small, is charged in layers with charcoal into a clay shaft furnace about a metre high and blown for hours at 1100–1300 °C. The iron never melts (that needs 1538 °C); it forms a spongy lump, the bloom, soaked in liquid slag. The bloom is pulled out white-hot and hammered to squeeze out the slag and weld it solid. The result is soft, tough wrought iron with almost no carbon, which can be forged and welded but not hardened. Packed in charcoal and held at a bright red heat for hours it takes up carbon at the surface and becomes steel.
- Pitfalls: Trying to melt and pour the iron as with bronze; in a bloomery it stays solid. | Too much blast or too tall a furnace makes brittle cast iron instead; too little heat leaves the ore unreduced. | Ore with much sulphur or phosphorus gives iron that cracks when hot or when cold. | Expecting quenching to harden wrought iron; without carbon nothing happens. | Underestimating the labour: roughly 10 kg of charcoal and a day's work for a kilogram of iron.
- History: egypt: c. 3200 BC – beads of hammered meteoritic iron (Gerzeh); smelted iron common only after c. 600 BC; mesopotamia: c. 2000–1200 BC – occasional smelted iron in Anatolia; the 'Hittite monopoly' is a legend; general use after c. 1200 BC; india: c. 1200 BC – iron in the Ganges plain and the south; dates as early as 1800 BC are claimed and disputed; greece: c. 1050 BC – iron replaces bronze for tools and weapons; china: c. 9th–8th c. BC – bloomery iron; cast iron follows within a few centuries and dominates; africa: c. 500 BC – Nok (Nigeria), Meroe and the Great Lakes; an independent invention and dates before 1000 BC are debated; europe: c. 800 BC – Hallstatt culture; the bloomery stays in use until the 18th–19th c. (Catalan forge); americas: Inuit cold-worked meteoritic iron from Cape York; around AD 1000 Norse settlers smelted bog iron at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland
- Read: R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976) | Radomír Pleiner, Iron in Archaeology: The European Bloomery Smelters (2000) | Vagn Fabritius Buchwald, Iron and Steel in Ancient Times (2005)

## Hardening and tempering steel `steel_heat_treatment`
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron
- Core idea: Medium- and high-carbon steels can be hardened by quenching. Heat the piece evenly into its austenitising range, which depends on composition. Loss of magnetic attraction near 770 °C is a rough guide, not a test of readiness, and plunge it into water or oil: it becomes glass-hard and brittle. Then polish a patch and reheat gently, watching the colour of the film that forms: pale straw (about 230 °C) for razors and cutting tools, brown-purple (260–280 °C) for axes and chisels, blue (about 300 °C) for springs and saws; quench again at the right colour. Slow cooling from red heat makes steel soft for filing.
- Pitfalls: Skipping the tempering; the tool snaps or chips at the first blow. | Believing the secret is in the quenching liquid (urine, blood, special springs); what matters is carbon content, temperature and speed. | Overheating to white, sparkling heat burns the steel and ruins it for good. | Expecting wrought iron to harden like tool steel; it contains too little carbon. Cast irons need heat treatments appropriate to their microstructure. | Quenching thin or uneven pieces carelessly; they warp and crack. Oil is gentler than water.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1100 BC – quench-hardened steel tools in Cyprus and the Levant; greece: c. 700 BC – the Odyssey (9.391) compares a hissing eye to a smith quenching an axe; india: by c. 500 BC – hardened steel tools and blades; china: by c. 3rd–2nd c. BC – quench-hardening of steel swords under the Qin and Han; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny notes that the water and oil used in quenching affect the result; europe: c. 1120 Theophilus describes hardening files; 1722 Réaumur studies steel fractures; 1863 Sorby sees the structure under the microscope
- Read: Cyril Stanley Smith, A History of Metallography (1960) | Theophilus, De diversis artibus (c. 1120; tr. Hawthorne & Smith, On Divers Arts, 1963)

## Cementation (blister) steel and case hardening `cementation_steel`
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron, charcoal_burning; helped by refractories_fireclay, steel_heat_treatment
- Core idea: Carbon soaks slowly into solid red-hot iron. For case hardening, pack finished iron parts in charcoal dust (with horn or leather scraps) in a sealed clay box and keep at orange heat for some hours: the skin becomes steel a millimetre deep and can be quenched hard over a tough core. For bar steel, pack wrought iron bars in charcoal in a sealed stone chest and fire at about 1050–1100 °C for five to seven days; the bars come out blistered and steely throughout, though unevenly, and are bundled, welded and forged to shear steel.
- Pitfalls: Letting air into the chest; the charcoal burns away and the iron scales instead of carburising. | Too long or too hot gives cast-iron-like, unforgeable bars. | Expecting uniform steel; the outside holds more carbon than the core until it is forged or melted. | Phosphoric or slaggy iron gives bad steel; Sheffield depended on pure Swedish bar iron.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1200–1000 BC – carburised iron tools in the Levant and Cyprus; china: c. 5th–6th c. AD – co-fusion steel (wrought iron soaked in molten cast iron), attributed to Qiwu Huaiwen; a different route to the same end; islamic: 9th–11th c. – al-Kindi and al-Biruni classify irons and steels and describe making steel in crucibles; europe: c. 1120 Theophilus case-hardens files; cementation furnaces at Prague (1574) and Nuremberg (1601); 1614 English patent; 1722 Réaumur publishes the process
- Read: René-Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur, L'art de convertir le fer forgé en acier (1722) | K. C. Barraclough, Steelmaking Before Bessemer (1984)

## Blast furnace and cast iron `blast_furnace_cast_iron`
- Deps: needs charcoal_burning, bellows_piston_blower; helped by water_wheel, refractories_fireclay, lime_burning, bloomery_iron
- Core idea: In a tall furnace (4 m and more) with a strong, continuous blast, the reduced iron stays long enough among glowing charcoal to take up 3–4.5 % carbon. That lowers its melting point to about 1150–1200 °C, so it collects as a liquid under the slag and can be tapped every few hours while ore, fuel and limestone flux are fed in at the top for months. Cast iron can be poured into pots, pipes, cannon and machine parts, but it is brittle and cannot be forged. To make bar iron, the carbon must be burnt out again in a second hearth (fining).
- Pitfalls: Treating cast iron like wrought iron; it shatters under the hammer and breaks under tension or shock. | A furnace that goes cold freezes solid and must be broken up; the campaign needs uninterrupted fuel, ore and blowing power. | Damp moulds or a wet tapping floor cause steam explosions. | Choosing the flux without considering the ore and fuel ash; some charges are self-fluxing, while others give a stiff slag without added flux. | White iron (cooled fast) is too hard to machine; grey iron needs slow cooling and silicon.
- History: china: c. 5th c. BC – cast iron tools and moulds (isolated pieces earlier); 117 BC Han state iron monopoly with large furnaces; AD 31 Du Shi's water-powered blowers; europe: c. 1150–1350 – Lapphyttan (Sweden) and the Märkisches Sauerland; 15th c. Walloon and Rhineland furnaces with finery forges; 1496 first English furnace (Weald); islamic: 11th c. – al-Biruni describes liquid 'dus' (cast iron) as an ingredient of crucible steel; no large blast-furnace industry is documented; africa: tall natural-draught furnaces in West and East Africa sometimes produced high-carbon iron; not a casting industry
- Read: Donald B. Wagner, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 11: Ferrous Metallurgy (2008) | R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)

## Smelting iron with coke `coke_iron`
- Deps: needs blast_furnace_cast_iron; helped by coal_mining, atmospheric_engine, refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: Raw coal spoils iron with sulphur and cakes in the furnace. Baked without air for a day or two in heaps or ovens, a suitable caking coal loses its tar and gas and part of its sulphur and becomes coke: hard, porous, nearly pure carbon. Coke carries a taller burden than charcoal, so furnaces can be much bigger, and it frees ironmaking from the forest. It needs a stronger blast (blowing cylinders driven by water or steam), more limestone to carry off the sulphur, and from 1828 a preheated blast that cut fuel use by about two thirds.
- Pitfalls: Assuming any coal will do; many coals do not coke or hold too much sulphur, which makes the iron crack when forged hot. | Using charcoal-sized bellows; coke will not burn hot enough without a harder blast. | Saying Darby's 1709 success changed the industry at once; early coke pig was sold mainly for castings; widespread use for bar iron came later. | Coke ovens and coal gas contain carbon monoxide; men died sleeping beside warm ovens.
- History: china: 11th c. – Song ironworks in the north use coal on a large scale; coke is probable but the evidence is thin. Coal-fired crucible smelting is documented later; europe: 1709 – Abraham Darby, Coalbrookdale; general in Britain only from the 1750s; 1784 puddling makes coke pig into bar iron; 1828 Neilson's hot blast; americas: 1830s–1850s – anthracite and then coke furnaces in Pennsylvania; india: 1875 – first lasting coke blast furnace at Kulti (Bengal)
- Read: Arthur Raistrick, Dynasty of Iron Founders: The Darbys and Coalbrookdale (1953) | Robert Hartwell, A Revolution in the Chinese Iron and Coal Industries during the Northern Sung, 960–1126 A.D., Journal of Asian Studies 21 (1962) | Joel Mokyr, The Lever of Riches (1990)

## Puddling and rolling (wrought iron from pig iron with coal) `puddling_wrought_iron`
- Deps: needs blast_furnace_cast_iron; helped by coke_iron, refractories_fireclay, trip_hammer_water_powered
- Core idea: Pig iron is melted on the hearth of a reverberatory furnace, where the coal burns in a separate grate and only the flame sweeps over the metal, so the fuel's sulphur stays out. The puddler stirs the bath with an iron bar; air and iron-oxide slag burn out the carbon, and because purer iron melts higher, the bath stiffens into pasty lumps. These are gathered into balls of about 40 kg, hammered to expel slag, and passed through grooved rolls into bars. One furnace gives a few tonnes a week of forgeable iron without charcoal.
- Pitfalls: Mixing fuel and metal as in a blast furnace; coal's sulphur ruins the iron. | A sand hearth wastes half the iron as slag; a bed of iron oxide (Hall's 'wet puddling') is far better. | Calling the product steel; it is fibrous wrought iron, soft and slag-streaked. | Thinking it can be scaled up freely; each heat depends on one man's strength and judgement, which is why Bessemer's process replaced it.
- History: china: c. 1st c. BC – Han ironworkers 'stir-fry' (chao) molten cast iron in open hearths to make wrought iron; europe: 15th c. finery forge with charcoal; 1766 Cranage brothers and 1783 Peter Onions anticipate parts of it; 1783–1784 Henry Cort's patents for grooved rolls and puddling; c. 1830 Joseph Hall's wet puddling; americas: a 2023 claim that Cort took the process from Black metalworkers in Jamaica has been examined and rejected by several historians; treat it as unsupported
- Read: Donald B. Wagner, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 11: Ferrous Metallurgy (2008) | R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)

## Crucible steel (wootz, Huntsman's cast steel) `crucible_steel`
- Deps: needs bloomery_iron, refractories_fireclay; helped by cementation_steel, coke_iron, bellows_piston_blower
- Core idea: Steel becomes uniform and free of slag only if it is fully melted. In the Indian method, small pieces of wrought iron are sealed in a clay crucible with charcoal or wood and leaves and fired for many hours in a strongly blown furnace until the iron has taken up 1–1.8 % carbon and melted to a small cake (wootz). Huntsman's method melts broken blister steel in fire-clay crucibles in a coke-fired draught furnace at about 1600 °C and pours it into an iron mould. The ingot is forged at a moderate red heat into blades, springs and tools.
- Pitfalls: Ordinary pottery crucibles slump long before steel melts; the refractory clay is the real secret. | Forging high-carbon wootz at a bright yellow heat makes it crumble; it must be worked at dull red. | Believing Damascus patterns come from folding; the classic watered blades are forged from a single crucible ingot, and the pattern depends on trace elements in the ore. | Thinking the quantities are large; a crucible gives one or two kilograms (later 15–25 kg).
- History: india: c. 300 BC or earlier – crucible steel in South India and Sri Lanka (Kodumanal, Mel-siruvalur); exported for two thousand years; islamic: 9th–11th c. – crucible steel at Merv and in Central Asia; al-Kindi and al-Biruni describe it; 'Damascus' blades forged from Indian and Persian ingots; china: co-fusion steel from the 5th–6th c. AD serves similar uses; true crucible steel is not the main tradition; europe: 8th–11th c. some Viking-age 'Ulfberht' swords appear to use imported crucible steel (debated); c. 1740 Benjamin Huntsman, Sheffield
- Read: Sharada Srinivasan & Srinivasa Ranganathan, India's Legendary Wootz Steel: An Advanced Material of the Ancient World (2004) | J. D. Verhoeven, A. H. Pendray & W. E. Dauksch, The Key Role of Impurities in Ancient Damascus Steel Blades, JOM 50 (1998) | K. C. Barraclough, Steelmaking Before Bessemer (1984)

## Bessemer steel (cheap bulk steel) `bessemer_steel`
- Deps: needs blast_furnace_cast_iron, refractories_fireclay; helped by coke_iron, high_pressure_steam, railway
- Core idea: Cold air blown through molten pig iron in a pear-shaped, tilting vessel burns out the silicon, manganese and carbon, and this burning itself supplies the heat: no fuel is needed and the metal gets hotter, not colder. Ten to twenty tonnes become steel in about twenty minutes instead of days. The blow is stopped when the flame drops, and a manganese-rich iron (spiegeleisen) is added to remove dissolved oxygen and set the carbon. With an ordinary silica lining the iron must be free of phosphorus; a lining of burnt dolomite with added lime (Thomas, 1879) takes the phosphorus into the slag.
- Pitfalls: Leaving out the manganese addition; the steel is full of oxygen and crumbles in forging. Bessemer's first licensees all failed on this. | Using phosphoric pig iron in an acid-lined converter; the steel is brittle when cold. Most European ores are phosphoric. | Blowing too long burns the iron itself; the end point is judged in seconds by the flame. | Saying it gave the first steel; it gave the first cheap steel in bulk. | Air-blown steel holds nitrogen and can be brittle, one reason the open hearth overtook it.
- History: europe: 1856 – Bessemer's paper at Cheltenham and Robert Mushet's manganese addition; 1858 Göransson makes it work in Sweden; 1878–1879 Thomas and Gilchrist's basic lining opens phosphoric ores; americas: 1847–1857 – William Kelly's air-blowing experiments in Kentucky; his priority claim won a US patent but his contribution is disputed; east_asia: 1901 – Yawata works (Japan); an older claim of a Japanese or Chinese air-refining forerunner rests on thin evidence
- Read: Henry Bessemer, Sir Henry Bessemer, F.R.S.: An Autobiography (1905) | Thomas J. Misa, A Nation of Steel: The Making of Modern America, 1865–1925 (1995)

## Open-hearth steel (Siemens-Martin) and the regenerative furnace `open_hearth_steel`
- Deps: needs blast_furnace_cast_iron, refractories_fireclay; helped by gas_lighting, coke_iron, bessemer_steel
- Core idea: A furnace gets much hotter if its waste gases preheat the incoming air and fuel gas. The hot exhaust is led through chambers stacked with firebrick; every twenty minutes or so the flow is reversed, so the air and gas now enter through the glowing bricks. This reaches about 1650 °C, enough to keep mild steel liquid on a shallow hearth. Pig iron is melted together with scrap or iron ore over eight to twelve hours, which leaves time to take samples and adjust the composition, and scrap can be reused.
- Pitfalls: Without silica bricks for the roof the furnace melts itself. | Forgetting the reversal; without it the regenerators do nothing. | Assuming faster is better; its advantage over Bessemer is control and the use of scrap, not speed. | Producer gas is rich in carbon monoxide; leaks in flues and valves kill.
- History: europe: 1856 – Friedrich and Wilhelm Siemens patent the regenerative furnace (first used for glass); 1864–1865 Pierre-Émile Martin makes steel in it at Sireuil; from the 1880s with a basic lining; the dominant steel process from c. 1900 to the 1960s; americas: 1868 – first American open hearth (Trenton); 1890s Carnegie converts to it
- Read: Thomas J. Misa, A Nation of Steel: The Making of Modern America, 1865–1925 (1995) | K. C. Barraclough, Steelmaking 1850–1900 (1990)

## Alloy, tool and stainless steels `alloy_stainless_steel`
- Deps: helped by crucible_steel, open_hearth_steel, electrolysis, lathe_screw_cutting
- Core idea: Small additions of other metals change steel greatly. About 12 % manganese gives a steel that hardens under blows (rail crossings, crusher jaws). Tungsten with chromium gives tool steel that keeps its edge at red heat and so cuts metal several times faster. Stainless steels contain at least about 10.5 % chromium and resist corrosion, because an invisible, self-healing chromium oxide film forms; 18 % chromium with 8 % nickel is the tough, formable kind. Chromium and nickel also give the strong steels needed for armour, engines and high-pressure vessels.
- Pitfalls: Judging corrosion resistance from chromium alone; composition, surface condition and the environment all affect the protective film. | Heat-treating high-speed steel like carbon steel; it must be quenched from near white heat (about 1250 °C) and tempered near 550 °C. | Stainless is not rust-proof in sea water or hot salt and acid; chlorides pit it. | The ores (chromite, wolframite, nickel) and ways to reduce them must exist first.
- History: india: c. AD 400 – the Delhi iron pillar resists rust through its high phosphorus content and dry climate, not through alloying; europe: 1819–1822 Faraday and Stodart, Berthier: experimental alloy steels; 1868 Mushet's self-hardening tungsten steel; 1882 Hadfield's manganese steel; 1912 Strauss and Maurer (Krupp), chromium-nickel stainless; 1913 Harry Brearley (Sheffield), chromium stainless cutlery steel; americas: 1898–1900 – Taylor and White's high-speed steel (Bethlehem); 1911–1912 Elwood Haynes's stainless alloys
- Read: Harold M. Cobb, The History of Stainless Steel (2010) | Thomas J. Misa, A Nation of Steel: The Making of Modern America, 1865–1925 (1995)

## Refractories (fireclay, crucibles, furnace linings) `refractories_fireclay`
- Deps: needs fired_brick_ceramics
- Core idea: Every hot process is limited by what the furnace and crucible are made of. Common red clay softens near 1100 °C. Pale fireclays rich in alumina and poor in iron, lime and alkali (often found under coal seams) stand 1500 °C and more, mixed with a third or more of crushed, already-fired clay (grog) so they do not shrink and crack. Crucibles gain from added graphite or charcoal dust. Silica bricks serve for the hottest furnace roofs; burnt dolomite or magnesite for linings that must resist limy slags. Dry everything for weeks and heat it slowly the first time.
- Pitfalls: Building a steel or glass furnace of ordinary brick; it melts or slags away in one firing. | Firing a damp lining or crucible; trapped steam bursts it, with molten metal inside. | Matching lining and slag wrongly: limy slags eat silica bricks, sandy slags eat dolomite. | Reusing a cracked crucible; a failed pot of molten metal maims.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 5000 BC – tempered clay crucibles and tuyères for copper; india: c. 300 BC – rice-husk-tempered crucibles for wootz that survive steel-melting heat; china: c. 1500 BC onwards – kaolin-rich kiln furniture and furnace linings for bronze, iron and high-fired ceramics; europe: 12th–18th c. – Hessian crucibles from Großalmerode, traded across Europe; graphite crucibles from Passau; 1822 silica (Dinas) brick in Wales; 1879 basic dolomite lining of Thomas and Gilchrist
- Read: Marcos Martinón-Torres, Thilo Rehren & Ian C. Freestone, Mullite and the mystery of Hessian wares, Nature 444 (2006) | R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)

## Brass and metallic zinc `zinc_brass`
- Deps: needs copper_bronze; helped by refractories_fireclay, distillation
- Core idea: Zinc boils at 907 °C, below the temperature at which charcoal reduces its ore, so in an ordinary furnace it leaves as vapour and burns to white smoke. Brass is therefore made without ever seeing zinc: heat small pieces of copper with roasted, ground calamine (zinc ore) and charcoal in a closed crucible at about 900–950 °C for many hours, and the zinc vapour soaks into the copper up to about 28–30 %; then raise the heat to melt and pour. To win the metal itself, heat the ore and charcoal in sealed clay retorts whose necks point downward into a cooler chamber, where the vapour condenses to drops.
- Pitfalls: Smelting zinc ore like copper or lead ore; all the metal is lost up the chimney. | Raising the crucible to copper's melting point too early; the zinc escapes before it is absorbed. | Breathing the white zinc fumes gives 'brass-founders' ague' (a day of fever and chills). | Confusing calamine with other white earths; test whether it turns copper golden. | Expecting brass to quench-harden; it hardens only by hammering.
- History: mesopotamia: 3rd–2nd millennium BC – occasional brass objects, probably accidental; 8th–7th c. BC deliberate cementation brass in Anatolia (Gordion); rome: c. 23 BC – Augustus's coinage reform uses orichalcum (brass) for sestertii and dupondii; india: c. 9th c. AD – zinc distilled by downward condensation at Zawar (Rajasthan), on an industrial scale by the 12th–16th c.; described in the Rasaratnakara and Rasarnava; china: 16th c. – zinc smelting under the Ming; exported to Europe as 'tutenag' in the 17th c.; islamic: 9th–12th c. – cementation brass (shabah) a major craft; tutty (zinc oxide) collected from furnaces; europe: medieval cementation brass at Dinant and Aachen; 1738 William Champion's patent for zinc distillation (Bristol); 1746 Marggraf describes the metal; africa: 9th–15th c. AD – leaded brass and bronze castings at Igbo-Ukwu, Ife and Benin
- Read: P. T. Craddock (ed.), 2000 Years of Zinc and Brass (1990) | R. F. Tylecote, A History of Metallurgy (1976)

## Cupellation, parting and assaying of silver and gold `cupellation_assaying`
- Deps: helped by bellows_piston_blower, nitric_acid, copper_bronze
- Core idea: Silver is mostly won from lead ores. The silver-bearing lead is melted in a shallow dish of bone ash or wood ash under a blast of air at about 900–1000 °C: the lead burns to litharge, which is absorbed by the ash or skimmed off, and a bright bead of silver (with any gold) is left. Gold is parted from silver by baking thin sheets with salt and brick dust for days, or by dissolving the silver out with nitric acid. Done on a carefully weighed sample, the same steps tell how much precious metal an ore or a coin contains.
- Pitfalls: Lead and litharge fumes poison the refiner; this was among the unhealthiest of old trades. | A dish of ordinary clay does not absorb litharge; it needs bone ash or leached wood ash. | Nitric acid parting fails if the alloy is more than about a quarter gold; silver must be added first (three parts to one). | Judging gold by colour or by a touchstone alone, which clever alloys can cheat.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3300 BC – litharge cakes from cupellation at Habuba Kabira (Syria); c. 550 BC gold and silver parted by salt cementation at Sardis for Croesus's coinage; greece: 5th c. BC – the Laurion mines and cupellation finance Athens; india: c. 300 BC – the Arthashastra describes state assayers and touchstone tests; china: by the Han – cupellation of silver; alchemical texts describe it; americas: c. AD 60–120 – silver refining from lead ores at Lake Titicaca, long before the Inca; europe: Roman Rio Tinto and medieval Freiberg and Kutná Hora; c. 14th–15th c. parting with nitric acid; 1556 Agricola and 1574 Ercker give full procedures
- Read: Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556; tr. H. C. Hoover & L. H. Hoover, 1912) | Lazarus Ercker, Treatise on Ores and Assaying (1574; tr. A. G. Sisco & C. S. Smith, 1951) | Andrew Ramage & Paul Craddock, King Croesus' Gold: Excavations at Sardis and the History of Gold Refining (2000)

## Mercury and amalgamation of gold and silver `mercury_amalgam`
- Deps: helped by distillation, salt_production
- Core idea: Red cinnabar roasted at about 600 °C gives mercury vapour, which condenses to the liquid metal on a cool surface. Mercury wets and dissolves gold and silver. Crushed gold ore or river sand is worked over mercury, the pasty amalgam is squeezed through leather and then heated in a closed retort, so the mercury distils off to be used again and the gold stays. For low-grade silver ore (patio process), the ground ore is spread wet in a yard and mixed with salt, roasted copper pyrites and mercury, trodden for weeks, washed, and the amalgam retorted. Gold amalgam brushed on to metal and heated gives fire gilding.
- Pitfalls: Mercury vapour has no smell and destroys nerves and kidneys; heating amalgam in the open poisons the worker and the household. Always distil in a closed retort outdoors. | It is not safe at room temperature either; spilt mercury in a warm room poisons slowly. | Mercury was long used as a medicine; it causes loosened teeth, tremor and madness rather than cure. | Expecting it to work on all ores; sulphide silver ores need salt and a copper salt, and some gold is too fine or coated to amalgamate. | Losing the mercury; it is dear, and about as much is lost as silver is won.
- History: china: c. 2nd millennium BC cinnabar as pigment; 210 BC rivers of mercury reported in the tomb of Qin Shi Huang; amalgam gilding by the Warring States period; greece: c. 300 BC – Theophrastus describes obtaining quicksilver from cinnabar; rome: 1st c. BC–1st c. AD – Vitruvius and Pliny describe recovering gold with mercury and fire gilding; mines at Almadén; islamic: 10th–12th c. – amalgamation of gold ores described (al-Hamdani, al-Biruni); Almadén worked under the caliphate; americas: cinnabar used as pigment in the pre-Columbian Andes and Mesoamerica; 1554 Bartolomé de Medina's patio process at Pachuca; 1570s adopted at Potosí with mercury from Huancavelica; europe: medieval fire gilding (Theophilus); 1540 Biringuccio describes amalgamating silver ore; 1887 the cyanide process begins to replace mercury
- Read: Vitruvius, De architectura VII.8 | Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540) | Nicholas A. Robins, Mercury, Mining, and Empire: The Human and Ecological Cost of Colonial Silver Mining in the Andes (2011)

## Lead is a cumulative poison `lead_hazard`
- Deps: helped by epidemiology_mapping, controlled_trial
- Core idea: Lead taken in small amounts over months builds up in the body and causes colic, constipation, pallor, gout, palsy of the wrists, miscarriage, and in children lasting damage to the mind. The worst sources are those that put it in food and drink: wine or must boiled down or sweetened in lead pans or with litharge ('sugar of lead' tastes sweet), cider and rum made in leaded equipment, lead-glazed and pewter vessels holding sour foods, white lead in paint and face powder. Lead pipes are most dangerous with soft or acid water. The proof is in comparison: the colic follows the leaded drink, not the district or the weather.
- Pitfalls: Saying lead pipes poisoned Rome and caused its fall; hard water scaled the pipes, the boiled-down grape syrup was the bigger source, and most historians reject the 'fall of Rome' thesis. | Assuming a poison must act quickly; lead works over months, which is why it went unnoticed. | Forgetting the makers: smelters, potters, painters and plumbers suffered most. | Offering no substitute; say what to use instead (tinned copper, glass, stoneware, clay or wooden pipes).
- History: greece: 2nd c. BC – Nicander describes poisoning by white lead and litharge; rome: c. 25 BC – Vitruvius advises clay pipes because lead workers are pallid; Pliny and Columella recommend lead pans for grape syrup all the same; china: lead and mercury elixirs poisoned alchemists and several Tang emperors (9th c.); white lead cosmetics in use from the Han; islamic: 10th–11th c. – Ibn Sina describes lead colic; europe: 1696 – Eberhard Gockel (Ulm) traces a colic epidemic to wine sweetened with litharge; 1700 Ramazzini on the diseases of potters and painters; 1767 George Baker proves Devonshire colic comes from lead in cider presses; americas: 1786 Franklin's letter on lead; 1923 leaded petrol introduced, phased out from the 1970s
- Read: Vitruvius, De architectura VIII.6 | George Baker, An Essay Concerning the Cause of the Endemial Colic of Devonshire (1767) | Jerome O. Nriagu, Lead and Lead Poisoning in Antiquity (1983)

## Soldering, brazing and tinning `soldering_tinning`
- Deps: helped by copper_bronze, zinc_brass
- Core idea: Metals are joined by a second metal that melts lower and wets both. Soft solder is tin with lead (the eutectic, about 63 % tin and 37 % lead by mass, melts at 183 °C; one tin to two lead stays pasty for wiping pipe joints); for hard joints use brass filings with borax at a bright red heat. The surfaces must be scraped bright and covered with a flux that keeps air off: tallow or rosin, sal ammoniac, or zinc dissolved in spirit of salt. Copper cooking vessels are tinned inside by wiping molten tin over the fluxed, heated metal, and thin iron sheet dipped in molten tin gives tinplate.
- Pitfalls: Dirty or oxidised metal: the solder balls up and the joint only looks sound. | Lead-bearing solder inside vessels and cans for food or drink poisons; use pure tin there. | Acid flux left on the work corrodes it; wash it off. Rosin is the safe flux for fine work. | Heating the solder instead of the work; the joint must be hot enough to melt the solder itself. | Untinned copper and brass pots give verdigris with sour food.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2500 BC – soldered gold and silver work in the royal graves of Ur; egypt: by c. 1400 BC – tin-lead and silver solders on jewellery and vessels; rome: 1st c. AD – Pliny describes tin-lead solders for pipes and the tinning of copper vessels, which he credits to the Gauls; china: by c. 5th c. BC – soldered joins on bronzes; tin-lead solders; europe: c. 1120 Theophilus gives solder and flux recipes; 14th c. tinplate made at Wunsiedel (Upper Franconia); 1720s–1730s rolled tinplate at Pontypool (Wales)
- Read: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis historia XXXIV.160–162 | Theophilus, De diversis artibus (c. 1120; tr. Hawthorne & Smith, On Divers Arts, 1963) | W. E. Minchinton, The British Tinplate Industry: A History (1957)

## Pottery, kilns and fired brick `fired_brick_ceramics`
- Deps: helped by charcoal_burning
- Core idea: Clay shaped wet and dried is still mud, but heated above about 600 °C it changes for good into a hard, water-resistant ceramic. Mix the clay with a fifth or more of sand, crushed shell or old potsherds so it shrinks evenly, dry it completely in the shade, then fire slowly: an open bonfire reaches 600–800 °C, and a kiln with a separate firebox, a perforated floor and a covered chamber reaches 900–1100 °C with far less fuel. Earthenware stays porous unless glazed; stoneware fired at 1200–1300 °C is dense. Fired bricks (length, width and thickness about 4:2:1) outlast sun-dried ones by centuries.
- Pitfalls: Firing ware that is not bone dry, or heating too fast: steam bursts it. | Pure, fat clay without temper cracks in drying; pebbles of limestone in the clay burn to lime and split the pot weeks later. | Lead glazes on vessels for wine, vinegar, fruit or cider poison the user. | Cooling the kiln quickly or opening it early cracks the whole load. | Underestimating fuel; a brick kiln eats several tonnes of wood for each firing.
- History: china: c. 18,000 BC – oldest known pottery (Xianrendong); kilns reach 1200 °C by the Shang; fired brick widespread from the Warring States period; east_asia: c. 14,000 BC – Jomon pottery in Japan; europe: c. 26,000 BC – fired clay figurines at Dolní Věstonice, long before pots; pottery from c. 6500 BC; africa: c. 9400 BC – pottery at Ounjougou (Mali), an independent invention; mesopotamia: c. 7000 BC pottery; c. 4000–3500 BC potter's wheel; c. 3100 BC fired brick at Uruk; 9th c. AD tin-opacified glaze at Basra; india: c. 2600 BC – standardised fired bricks in the Indus cities; americas: c. 5500 BC – pottery in the lower Amazon (Taperinha), independent of the Old World; egypt: c. 4000 BC – glazed faience; fired brick rare before the Roman period
- Read: Prudence M. Rice, Pottery Analysis: A Sourcebook (1987) | Xiaohong Wu et al., Early Pottery at 20,000 Years Ago in Xianrendong Cave, China, Science 336 (2012) | James W. P. Campbell & Will Pryce, Brick: A World History (2003)

## Porcelain `porcelain`
- Deps: needs fired_brick_ceramics; helped by refractories_fireclay
- Core idea: A traditional Jingdezhen hard-paste porcelain body combines kaolin, a white clay that does not melt, and china stone (a feldspar-rich rock, ground fine), which melts and binds it. Roughly equal parts are shaped, usually glazed with china stone mixed with lime or ash, and fired at 1280–1400 °C in a kiln that can hold that heat for a day, with a smoky, air-starved flame at the peak so that traces of iron do not turn it yellow. The body becomes white, dense, ringing and translucent where thin. The ware is stacked in fireclay boxes (saggars) to keep off ash and flame.
- Pitfalls: Confusing ceramic bodies: some European soft-paste porcelains use glass frit, while bone china uses calcined bone ash with clay and a flux. Their firing behaviour differs from hard paste. | Believing the old tales that it is made from eggshells or shells buried for a century. | A common pottery kiln stops near 1000–1100 °C; porcelain needs a different kiln and firebricks. | Any iron in the clay or water spots the ware; kaolin deposits must be sought (Saxony, Cornwall, Limoges).
- History: china: c. 1600 BC high-fired 'proto-porcelain'; c. 2nd c. AD Eastern Han porcelain in Zhejiang; c. 600 white porcelain (Xing ware); from c. 1000 Jingdezhen; 14th c. blue-and-white; east_asia: c. 10th c. Korea (celadon, then white porcelain); 1616 Arita, Japan, by tradition founded by Korean potters; islamic: 9th c. tin-glazed imitations in Iraq; 11th–12th c. stonepaste (fritware) bodies in Egypt and Iran; europe: 1575–1587 Medici soft-paste porcelain, Florence; 1708 Tschirnhaus and Böttger make hard-paste porcelain in Saxony, Meissen factory 1710; 1712 and 1722 letters of Père d'Entrecolles describe Jingdezhen
- Read: Rose Kerr & Nigel Wood, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 12: Ceramic Technology (2004) | Janet Gleeson, The Arcanum: The Extraordinary True Story (1998)

## Glassmaking and glassblowing `glassmaking`
- Deps: helped by alkali_soda, lime_burning, refractories_fireclay, charcoal_burning
- Core idea: A typical soda-lime glass contains three main oxides, supplied by sand or crushed quartz (about 65–70 %), an alkali that makes it melt (soda or plant ash, about 15–20 %) and lime (about 10 %) that makes it stand up to water. Roast the mixed batch for hours at dull red heat (fritting), then melt it in fireclay pots at 1100–1300 °C until the bubbles rise out. A gather taken on the end of an iron tube about 1.3 m long can be blown, swung and shaped while it stays orange-hot. Finished pieces must cool slowly over many hours in a chamber at about 500 °C, or they shatter later. Broken glass added to the batch helps it melt.
- Pitfalls: Sand alone will not melt in any wood-fired furnace (it needs about 1700 °C). | Leaving out the lime gives a glass that clouds, weeps and finally dissolves in water. | Skipping the slow cooling; the piece cracks hours or days later, sometimes violently. | Ordinary sand contains iron and gives green or brown glass. | Pots that fail in the furnace; glassmaking stands or falls with the fireclay.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2500 BC – first glass beads; c. 1500 BC core-formed vessels; c. 50 BC glassblowing invented on the Syro-Palestinian coast; egypt: c. 1500 BC – glass vessels and ingots (Amarna, Qantir); earlier faience; india: c. 1000 BC – glass beads; large bead industries by the last centuries BC; china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – lead-barium glass, a separate recipe; blown glass arrives with imports in the Han period; rome: 1st c. AD – blown vessels cheap and common; window panes; islamic: 8th–14th c. – plant-ash glass, cutting, lustre painting, enamelled and gilded glass in Syria and Egypt; africa: 11th–15th c. – glass made from local materials at Ile-Ife (Nigeria); europe: medieval potash 'forest glass'; 1291 Venetian furnaces moved to Murano; 1612 Neri prints the first book of glass recipes
- Read: Antonio Neri, L'arte vetraria (1612) | Theophilus, De diversis artibus (c. 1120; tr. Hawthorne & Smith, On Divers Arts, 1963) | Julian Henderson, Ancient Glass: An Interdisciplinary Exploration (2013)

## Colourless and optical glass (cristallo, lead crystal, plate) `clear_glass`
- Deps: needs glassmaking; helped by alkali_soda, refractories_fireclay, lenses
- Core idea: Glass is green because of iron in the sand and dirty because of the ash. Venetian cristallo used crushed white quartz pebbles instead of sand, plant ash that was dissolved, filtered and recrystallised to a white salt (with some lime put back), and a pinch of manganese ore, whose faint purple cancels the last green. Lead glass (about one third red lead) is heavier, more brilliant and bends light more strongly. For lenses the melt must also be free of streaks and bubbles, which is achieved by stirring it with a fireclay rod while it cools; a crown glass lens paired with a lead glass lens removes colour fringes.
- Pitfalls: Too much manganese turns the glass pink or purple; sunlight later does the same. | Over-purified ash loses its lime and the glass slowly crizzles and decays, as Ravenscroft's first lead-free batches did. | A clear-looking glass may still be full of streaks that ruin a lens; hold it against a sharp edge of light to check. | Lead glass must be melted in covered pots away from smoke or it turns black. | Polished plate takes weeks of grinding with sand and emery; blown window glass is never flat.
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – glass decolourised with antimony or manganese, prized above gold cups according to Pliny; islamic: 9th–10th c. – clear cut glass in Iraq and Iran; rock crystal carving in Fatimid Egypt; china: lead glasses known from the Warring States; clear optical glass arrives with Jesuit workshops in the 1690s; europe: c. 1450 Angelo Barovier's cristallo (Murano); 1674–1676 Ravenscroft's lead crystal; 1688 cast plate glass at Saint-Gobain; 1758 Dollond's achromatic lens; c. 1805 Guinand's stirring; 1884 Schott's Jena glass; 1959 float glass (Pilkington)
- Read: Antonio Neri, L'arte vetraria (1612) | W. Patrick McCray, Glassmaking in Renaissance Venice: The Fragile Craft (1999)

## Glass mirrors (tin amalgam and silvering) `glass_mirrors`
- Deps: needs glassmaking; helped by clear_glass, mercury_amalgam, nitric_acid
- Core idea: A flat, clear glass plate backed with bright metal gives a far better image than polished bronze. The old method: smooth a sheet of tin foil on a level stone table, flood it with mercury, slide the cleaned glass across so no air is trapped, weight it, and tilt the table over some weeks to drain the surplus; a tin amalgam layer stays on the glass. The modern method deposits real silver: a solution of silver nitrate in ammonia, mixed with a reducing sugar or tartrate, coats clean glass in minutes; a coat of varnish or copper protects it.
- Pitfalls: Mercury mirror workers suffered tremor, lost teeth and early death; the method needs ventilation and is best avoided. | Ammonia-silver solution that is kept or allowed to dry forms a compound that explodes at a touch; mix it fresh and wash the remains away at once. | Any grease on the glass leaves bare patches; clean with nitric acid or lye and pure water. | Wavy or greenish glass gives a distorted, dark image whatever the coating. | Pouring molten metal on cold glass cracks it; early lead-backed mirrors were made on thin, hot, blown bulbs and are small and convex.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 6000 BC – polished obsidian mirrors at Çatalhöyük; from c. 3000 BC polished copper and bronze; egypt: from c. 2900 BC – polished copper and bronze hand mirrors; china: c. 2000 BC bronze mirrors (Qijia culture); high-tin mirrors a major craft from the Warring States to the Tang; americas: c. 1000 BC – Olmec concave mirrors of polished magnetite and ilmenite; later pyrite and obsidian; rome: 1st–3rd c. AD – small convex glass mirrors backed with lead; europe: 13th–15th c. convex lead-backed glass mirrors (Nuremberg); 1507 Venetian privilege for flat tin-amalgam mirrors (dal Gallo brothers); 1835 Liebig observes silver deposition, industrial after 1856; 1857 Foucault's silvered telescope mirror; 1930s vacuum-deposited aluminium
- Read: Sabine Melchior-Bonnet, The Mirror: A History (2001) | Per Hadsund, The Tin-Mercury Mirror: Its Manufacturing Technique and Deterioration Processes, Studies in Conservation 38 (1993)

## Hydraulic lime, Roman concrete and Portland cement `hydraulic_cement`
- Deps: needs lime_burning; helped by fired_brick_ceramics, coke_iron
- Core idea: Lime mortar that contains reactive silica and alumina hardens by reaction with water, even under water. Vitruvius specifies two parts volcanic ash (pozzolana) to one of lime for harbour work. His three-to-one ratio for ordinary mortar refers to pit sand; finely crushed brick or tile serves where there is no volcano. The same effect comes from burning limestone that naturally contains clay. Portland cement is made by grinding limestone and clay together (about four to one), burning the mix until it begins to fuse at about 1450 °C, and grinding the clinker fine with a few per cent of gypsum. Concrete is cement, sand and gravel at about 1:2:4 with as little water as will work, kept damp for a week.
- Pitfalls: Saying it 'dries'; it sets by taking up water and is ruined if it dries out or freezes while young. | Too much water makes weak, porous concrete. | Any grey powder will not do: ordinary sand or ash is inert, and the pozzolan must be tested with lime under water. | Burning at lime-kiln heat gives only weak hydraulic lime; true cement needs near-white heat and hard grinding. | The myth that the Roman recipe was lost and is stronger than modern concrete; it is durable but much weaker and slower.
- History: greece: c. 500–300 BC – lime with volcanic earth from Thera or crushed tile in cisterns (Kameiros, Rhodes); rome: c. 200 BC – pozzolana concrete in Campania; c. 20 BC Vitruvius and the harbour of Caesarea; c. AD 126 the Pantheon dome; india: ancient to Mughal – lime with brick dust (surkhi) for tanks and waterworks; islamic: medieval – lime with ash and crushed brick (sarooj) for cisterns, baths and bridges in Iran; europe: 1756–1759 Smeaton finds that clayey limestone gives hydraulic lime (Eddystone); 1796 Parker's 'Roman cement'; 1818 Vicat's artificial hydraulic lime; 1824 Aspdin's Portland cement patent; c. 1845 Isaac Johnson burns it to clinker, the modern product
- Read: Vitruvius, De architectura II.6 and V.12 | John Smeaton, A Narrative of the Building and a Description of the Construction of the Edystone Lighthouse with Stone (1791) | Marie D. Jackson et al., Phillipsite and Al-tobermorite mineral cements produced through low-temperature water-rock reactions in Roman marine concrete, American Mineralogist 102 (2017)

## Reinforced concrete `reinforced_concrete`
- Deps: needs hydraulic_cement; helped by puddling_wrought_iron, bessemer_steel, wire_drawing
- Core idea: Concrete resists crushing well but tears apart under a tenth of that load in tension. A beam bends so that its underside is stretched, so iron or steel rods are cast into the stretched side: near the bottom in the middle of a span, near the top over supports and in cantilevers, with hooked ends and thin stirrups around them. It works because cement grips the rough bars, their thermal expansion rates are similar, and alkaline concrete passivates the steel. The cover needed depends on exposure; cracks, carbonation and chlorides can break down that protection.
- Pitfalls: Putting the bars in the middle or on the wrong side; the beam cracks and falls as if unreinforced. | Sea sand, sea water or salt in the mix rusts the bars, and the rust bursts the concrete. | Too little cover, or porous concrete, has the same result after some years. | Removing the formwork and props too early; give it weeks, not days. | Assuming Roman concrete was reinforced; it works in compression only (arches, vaults, domes).
- History: europe: 1848 Lambot's wire-reinforced boat; 1853 Coignet's iron-and-concrete house; 1854 Wilkinson's English patent for reinforced floors; 1867 Monier's patent (flower tubs, then pipes and bridges); 1892 Hennebique's system of beams and stirrups; 1928 Freyssinet's prestressed concrete; americas: 1884 Ransome's twisted bar; 1903 Ingalls Building, Cincinnati, the first reinforced-concrete tall building
- Read: Peter Collins, Concrete: The Vision of a New Architecture (1959) | Robert Courland, Concrete Planet (2011)

## Papermaking `paper`
- Deps: helped by textile_fibres, trip_hammer_water_powered, water_wheel, lime_burning
- Core idea: Paper is a felt of separated plant fibres. Take old linen or hemp rags (or the inner bark of mulberry), rot them for some weeks, boil with lime or ash lye and beat them in water for hours until they form a milky pulp of single fibres. Dip a flat sieve (a frame strung with fine wire or bamboo) into the vat, lift it level and shake it; turn the wet sheet out on a woollen felt, stack, press hard, and hang to dry. Dipping the sheets in thin animal glue or starch keeps ink from spreading. Water-driven stamp mills do the beating.
- Pitfalls: Confusing it with papyrus (strips laid crosswise) or parchment (skin); neither is paper. | Sawdust or straw mashed in water gives no paper; wood needs grinding or cooking in chemicals, known only from the 1840s. | Unsized sheets blot; under-beaten pulp gives lumpy, weak sheets. | Iron in the water or the stampers leaves rust spots. | Forgetting that rags run short once paper is in demand; the supply of fibre is the limit.
- History: china: 2nd c. BC – hemp paper fragments (Fangmatan, Baqiao); AD 105 Cai Lun reports an improved process to the court, the traditional but not the true date of invention; east_asia: c. 3rd–4th c. Korea and Vietnam; AD 610 by tradition brought to Japan by the monk Damjing; islamic: 8th c. – paper mills at Samarkand (the story of prisoners taken at Talas in 751 is a later legend) and 794–795 Baghdad; rag paper with starch sizing; india: known from the 7th–8th c.; common from the 13th c. under the Delhi sultanate; americas: by c. AD 300 – Maya and later Aztec amate, a beaten bark sheet, made independently; not true paper; europe: 11th–12th c. Spain (Xàtiva) and Sicily; c. 1270 Fabriano introduces water-powered stampers, gelatine sizing and watermarks; 1798 Robert's paper machine; 1844 Keller's ground-wood pulp
- Read: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing (1985) | Jonathan M. Bloom, Paper Before Print: The History and Impact of Paper in the Islamic World (2001) | Dard Hunter, Papermaking: The History and Technique of an Ancient Craft (1943)

## Preparing textile fibres (wool, flax, cotton, silk) `textile_fibres`
- Deps: helped by sericulture, soap, cotton_gin
- Core idea: Every fibre must be cleaned, freed and aligned before spinning. Wool is washed of grease, then carded (short, fluffy yarn) or combed (long, smooth yarn); woven wool cloth is pounded in water with fuller's earth or stale urine to felt and thicken it. Flax stems are rotted in water or dew for one to three weeks (retting), dried, broken, scraped and drawn through combs. Cotton is seeded, beaten open and carded; its short hairs need a fast spindle. Silk is unwound as one continuous thread from cocoons floating in hot water, several together. Twist is what turns loose fibre into strong yarn.
- Pitfalls: Over-retting flax rots the fibre itself; under-retting leaves it stuck to the stem. | Letting the silk moth hatch cuts the thread; the cocoons must be stifled by heat first. | Expecting European spinners used to wool to spin cotton fine and strong; warp-quality cotton yarn was an Indian skill. | Retting ponds foul drinking water and fish streams. | Raw wool and hides can carry anthrax ('woolsorters' disease').
- History: mesopotamia: 7th millennium BC woven oak-bast textiles at Çatalhöyük in Anatolia; c. 4000–3000 BC woolly sheep and a large wool industry; egypt: c. 5000 BC – linen; very fine linen weaving by the Old Kingdom; india: c. 5500–5000 BC cotton fibres at Mehrgarh; cotton cloth at Mohenjo-daro c. 2500 BC; americas: c. 5000–4000 BC – cotton independently domesticated in Peru and, as another species, in Mexico; camelid wool in the Andes; china: c. 3600–2700 BC – silk (cut cocoon at Xiyin, fabric at Qianshanyang); hemp and ramie older; africa: by c. 1st c. AD – cotton grown and woven in Nubia (Meroe); raffia and bark cloth elsewhere; europe: Neolithic flax and later wool; c. AD 552 silkworm eggs reach Byzantium; cotton via Islamic Sicily and Spain from the 9th–12th c.
- Read: E. J. W. Barber, Prehistoric Textiles: The Development of Cloth in the Neolithic and Bronze Ages (1991) | Antoinette Rast-Eicher, Sabine Karg & Lise Bender Jørgensen, The use of local fibres for textiles at Neolithic Çatalhöyük, Antiquity 95 (2021) | Sven Beckert, Empire of Cotton: A Global History (2014)

## Tanning leather `leather_tanning`
- Deps: helped by lime_burning
- Core idea: A raw hide rots when wet and turns to horn when dry; tanning makes it permanent. Soak the hide for a week or two in lime water until the hair slips, scrape hair and flesh off, wash the lime out again (traditionally with a ferment of dung or bran), then lay the hides in pits with ground oak bark and water, moving them into stronger liquor over six to eighteen months. Finally work in oil or tallow. Quick alternatives are alum with salt (white, soft leather that is not waterproof), smoking with brains or fat, and from the 1880s chromium salts, which tan in a day.
- Pitfalls: Putting hides straight into strong bark liquor; the surface tans hard and seals the inside raw. | Leaving lime in the hide; the leather turns brittle. | Hides carry anthrax; tanners and wool workers died of it. | Tannery waste poisons wells and streams; site it downstream and downwind. | Mistaking alum-tawed skin for true leather; it reverts to rawhide when soaked.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3500 BC – a leather shoe from Areni-1 (Armenia); cuneiform recipes use alum, gall nuts and fat; europe: c. 3300 BC – Ötzi's fat- and smoke-treated clothing; Roman military tanneries; 1858 Knapp describes chrome tanning; egypt: c. 1450 BC – leather workshop scenes in the tomb of Rekhmire; vegetable tanning becomes general in the Graeco-Roman period; india: ancient – tanning with myrobalan and babul bark; islamic: 8th–12th c. – fine goat leathers of Córdoba and Morocco (cordovan, morocco); americas: ancient – brain and smoke tanning of deer and bison hides; 1884 Augustus Schultz's chrome tanning patent
- Read: R. Reed, Ancient Skins, Parchments and Leathers (1972) | Ron Pinhasi et al., First Direct Evidence of Chalcolithic Footwear from the Near Eastern Highlands, PLoS ONE 5 (2010)

## Aluminium `aluminium`
- Deps: helped by electrolysis, dynamo_electric_motor, alkali_soda, water_turbine
- Core idea: Aluminium is the commonest metal in the earth's crust (in every clay), but it holds oxygen so tightly that charcoal cannot reduce it in any ordinary furnace. The first metal was made by chemical reduction of aluminium chloride. Bulk production uses electrolysis: pure alumina, extracted from bauxite with hot caustic soda, is dissolved in molten cryolite at about 950–980 °C in a carbon-lined steel cell, and a very large current at a few volts deposits liquid aluminium on the floor while the carbon anodes burn away. It takes about 15 kWh for each kilogram, so the works stand beside cheap water power. The metal is a third the weight of steel and does not rust through.
- Pitfalls: Electrolysing a solution in water; only hydrogen comes off. | Confusing laboratory and factory scale: Hall obtained small samples with batteries; continuous bulk production needs a large, cheap current supply. | Trying to smelt clay or bauxite with charcoal. | Pure aluminium is soft; aircraft and structures need alloys (duralumin, with about 4 % copper, hardens by ageing after solution treatment and quenching). | The tale of a Roman who showed Tiberius an unbreakable metal from clay, and the 'aluminium' belt from a 3rd-century Chinese tomb, are not evidence of ancient aluminium.
- History: europe: 1825 Ørsted and 1827 Wöhler isolate it chemically; 1854 Deville's sodium process makes it a luxury metal; 1886 Paul Héroult's electrolytic process; 1887–1888 Bayer process for alumina; 1906–1909 Wilm's duralumin; americas: 1886 – Charles Martin Hall, independently of Héroult; 1888 Pittsburgh Reduction Company (later Alcoa)
- Read: Joseph W. Richards, Aluminium: Its History, Occurrence, Properties, Metallurgy and Applications (1887) | Mimi Sheller, Aluminum Dreams: The Making of Light Modernity (2014)

## Wood tar and pitch `wood_tar_pitch`
- Deps: helped by charcoal_burning
- Core idea: Wood heated with almost no air does not burn but chars, and the water and tarry vapours are driven off. Resinous wood charred in a sloping pit or kiln runs out tar, which boils down to pitch for ships, ropes and barrels.
- Pitfalls: Too much air turns the whole stack to ash. | Drinking the watery distillate; it contains wood spirit (methanol), which blinds.
- History: europe: c. 200,000 years ago – birch tar survives on stone tools at Campitello, Italy; the finds show adhesive use but do not identify the production method; 17th–18th c. Swedish 'Stockholm tar' supplies Europe's navies; greece: c. 300 BC – Theophrastus describes Macedonian pitch burning
- Read: Theophrastus, Enquiry into Plants IX.3 | Paul Peter Anthony Mazza et al., A new Palaeolithic discovery: tar-hafted stone tools in a European Mid-Pleistocene bone-bearing bed, Journal of Archaeological Science 33 (2006) | Lewis Dartnell, The Knowledge: How to Rebuild Our World from Scratch (2014)
